interest: Japanese espionage against the Soviets and a Nomonhan propaganda trick.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.20261) consists of diplomatic despatches, an internal memorandum, and a cross-reference sheet spanning 1934 to 1939 that document Japanese military intelligence activities, espionage networks, and propaganda operations directed against the Soviet Union. The primary records focus on the tense borderlands between the Soviet Far East and Japanese-dominated Manchukuo. Key materials include a 1934 cross-reference sheet concerning alleged Japanese secret agent D. F. Giera; a detailed 1936 despatch from U.S. Ambassador William C. Bullitt in Moscow analyzing the Soviet public trial in Khabarovsk of twenty-one Japanese spies (predominantly Koreans) and related cross-border intelligence skirmishes and torture; and 1939 reports from American Consul George R. Merrell in Harbin detailing a clumsy Japanese gendarmerie scheme to trick departing French Consul Jules Leurquin into carrying pro-Japanese Nomonhan war propaganda across Siberia.

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the Soviet public espionage trial of twenty-one Japanese agents in Khabarovsk and broader Soviet-Japanese intelligence operations and border clashes.
subfiles.from: William C. Bullitt (U.S. Ambassador to the Soviet Union, Moscow)
subfiles.summary: Ambassador William C. Bullitt transmits a detailed summary of the public espionage trial held in Khabarovsk, drawing on a six-part serial in the newspaper Tikhookeanskaya Zvezda (Pacific Ocean Star) by correspondent L. Reshetov. The trial prosecuted twenty-one defendants—twenty stateless Koreans and one Russian émigré directed from Manchukuo—accused of infiltrating Soviet territory to map airfields and munitions factories and smuggle military gear such as gas masks, financed in part by opium contraband. Bullitt includes commentary from Japanese Embassy Counselor Tsuneo Sakoh, who characterized the trial as political theater while acknowledging reciprocal espionage and coercive interrogations by both sides. The despatch also highlights a report from Pravda detailing the severe interrogation torture and subsequent release of a Soviet citizen, Pirogov, arrested by Manchukuoan police.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1458 from Ambassador Bullitt on Khabarovsk Espionage Trial
